blocks.title: A 58-Year-Old with Fatigue, Iron-Deficiency Anaemia, and Obstruction
blocks.scenario: A 58-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 4-month history of progressive fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion. Labs reveal haemoglobin 8.2 g/dL with microcytic, hypochromic indices and ferritin of 6 ng/mL. On further questioning, he endorses intermittent left lower quadrant cramping and a perceived change in stool calibre over the same period. He has no prior colonoscopy, no family history of CRC, and is otherwise without significant medical history. Colonoscopy demonstrates a near-obstructing, ulcerated mass in the sigmoid colon. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis shows no distant metastases but reveals three enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Final pathology after sigmoid colectomy: moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, T3N2aM0 — AJCC 8th edition Stage IIIC. Tumour is sent for reflex MMR immunohistochemistry and BRAF V600E testing.
blocks.learning_hook: Why does this patient's MSI/MMR status fundamentally change both the adjuvant treatment decision and the germline counselling pathway — and what do the perioperative data say about prophylactic HIPEC in patients like him?

blocks.title: Global Incidence and Mortality Trends
blocks.content: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most commonly diagnosed malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, with approximately 1.9 million new cases and 935,000 deaths reported annually. Incidence rates have declined steadily in adults over 50 in high-income countries, attributable largely to the uptake of screening colonoscopy and polypectomy — an intervention that interrupts the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. Paradoxically, incidence among adults younger than 50 has risen approximately 1–2% per year over the past two decades in the United States and several European nations, a trend not yet fully explained but implicating dietary patterns, obesity, and alterations in the gut microbiome. Stage III disease — regional lymph node involvement without distant metastases — accounts for roughly 25–30% of newly diagnosed CRC cases, and this cohort carries a 5-year overall survival of approximately 40–80% depending on T and N substage.

blocks.title: AJCC 8th Edition Stage III Substaging and Approximate 5-Year Survival
Hereditary, Familial, and Sporadic Risk Pathways
blocks.content: Approximately 75% of CRC cases are sporadic, arising in individuals without a recognised hereditary syndrome or strong family history, with cumulative environmental exposures — processed red meat intake, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic alcohol use, and tobacco — driving adenoma formation and malignant progression. Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis CRC), caused by germline pathogenic variants in MMR genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), accounts for 3–5% of all CRC and is the most clinically actionable hereditary syndrome because of its implications for surveillance, extracolonic cancer risk, and — critically — adjuvant treatment selection. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), driven by germline APC mutations, accounts for less than 1% of CRC but carries near-100% lifetime penetrance without prophylactic colectomy. For the practising surgeon, the diagnostic index of suspicion for Lynch syndrome must be highest in patients presenting under age 50, with right-sided tumours, MSI-H pathology, or a personal/family history of Lynch-associated cancers (endometrial, ovarian, urinary tract, small bowel).

blocks.title: Do Not Miss Lynch Syndrome Reflexively
blocks.content: A resident orders MMR IHC on a 58-year-old's sigmoid tumour, finds MSI-H / MLH1-loss, and immediately refers for germline Lynch syndrome counselling — but the concurrent BRAF V600E mutation is not noticed. In MSI-H CRC where BRAF V600E is also present, the mechanism is almost always sporadic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation (CIMP-high), not Lynch syndrome germline mutation. Reflexive MLH1 promoter methylation testing must be ordered first; if methylation is confirmed, germline testing is not indicated and unnecessary patient anxiety is avoided. Lynch syndrome workup should proceed only when BRAF is wild-type or methylation is absent.

blocks.title: Screening, Polyp Biology, and the Adenoma-Carcinoma Sequence
blocks.content: The foundational rationale for CRC screening rests on the adenoma-carcinoma sequence: conventional adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous) accumulate stepwise mutations over 10–15 years, while serrated lesions (sessile serrated adenomas/polyps) progress more rapidly via a BRAF V600E–driven, CIMP-associated epigenetic pathway. Colonoscopy with polypectomy reduces CRC incidence and mortality by interrupting this sequence before invasive transformation. High-quality colonoscopy — defined by an adenoma detection rate ≥25% in average-risk populations — is the benchmark quality metric because each 1% increase in ADR is associated with a measurable reduction in post-colonoscopy interval cancer. Faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) and multi-target stool DNA testing are acceptable non-invasive screening alternatives in average-risk patients but require colonoscopic follow-up for any positive result. For Lynch syndrome carriers, annual or biennial colonoscopy beginning at age 20–25 (or 2–5 years before the earliest affected relative) is the standard surveillance interval.

blocks.title: Iron-Deficiency Anaemia in a Man Over 50 Is a Colon Cancer Until Proven Otherwise
blocks.content: In the absence of an obvious bleeding source (e.g., heavy menstrual loss), unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in any man or any post-menopausal woman over 50 mandates bidirectional endoscopic evaluation. Right-sided colon cancers classically present with occult blood loss and anaemia rather than obstructive symptoms because the right colon lumen is wide and stool is liquid — a tumour can reach significant size before obstruction occurs. Missing this presentation by attributing anaemia to dietary causes or treating empirically with iron alone is a preventable diagnostic delay.

points: Stage III CRC (T any, N1–N2, M0) spans substages IIIA–IIIC with 5-year OS ranging from ~25% to ~80%; substage guides prognostic counselling and adjuvant chemotherapy duration decisions.

Lynch syndrome accounts for 3–5% of all CRC; reflex MMR immunohistochemistry or MSI testing on all newly diagnosed CRC is recommended to identify candidates for germline counselling and to guide adjuvant therapy.
BRAF V600E co-occurring with MSI-H/MLH1 loss strongly suggests sporadic, CIMP-high CRC from MLH1 promoter methylation — order reflexive methylation testing before initiating germline workup.
The rise in CRC incidence among adults under 50 has lowered the threshold for investigation of lower GI symptoms in younger patients; age alone should not be used to defer endoscopic evaluation.
Right-sided tumours are enriched for MSI-H and BRAF V600E; awareness of this molecular geography informs both prognosis and downstream metastatic treatment planning even at Stage III diagnosis.

Adequate lymph node harvest (≥12 nodes) at the index oncologic resection is a non-negotiable quality metric — failure to achieve this compromises staging accuracy and may lead to understaging and undertreated disease.

blocks.title: Anatomía quirúrgica y embriología
blocks.content: El colon y el recto derivan del intestino medio y posterior, separados embriológicamente por el punto de unión entre los territorios de la arteria mesentérica superior (AMS) y la arteria mesentérica inferior (AMI). Esta frontera, localizada en la unión del tercio proximal con el tercio medio del colon transverso, determina tanto los pedículos vasculares de resección como los patrones de drenaje linfático. La comprensión de estos planos embriológicos es el fundamento de la resección oncológica con margen de mesocolon completo (CME) y de la escisión total del mesorrecto (TME).

blocks.title: Planos fasciales: la clave de la resección oncológica
blocks.content: La fascia de Toldt representa la fusión del mesocolon posterior con el peritoneo parietal retroperitoneal durante la rotación intestinal fetal. Disecar en este plano avascular — inmediatamente anterior a la fascia de Gerota y a los uréteres — permite la movilización del colon sin invadir el mesocolon ni fragmentarlo. En el recto, el plano análogo es el plano areolar perirrectal, delimitado por la fascia mesorrectal (visceral) y la fascia presacra (parietal). La TME requiere disección precisa dentro de este plano para garantizar un margen circunferencial (CRM) libre de tumor. La violación de la fascia mesorrectal durante la resección es el predictor independiente más fuerte de recidiva local en cáncer de recto.

blocks.title: El plano de Toldt no se 'busca' — se reconoce
blocks.content: El plano de Toldt correcto es brillante, blanquecino y completamente avascular. Si hay sangrado, o si se visualizan fibras musculares o la grasa perirrenal, el plano es incorrecto. Redirigir la disección medialmente antes de continuar.

blocks.title: Alta ligadura de AMI: riesgo de isquemia del colon izquierdo residual
blocks.content: Cuando se realiza alta ligadura de la AMI en resecciones rectales, la vascularización del colon izquierdo depende exclusivamente del arco de Riolano y la arteria marginal de Drummond. Si la arteria cólica media tiene un territorio reducido o la arcada marginal es incompleta — variante presente en ~5% de pacientes — el extremo proximal del colon descendente puede quedar isquémico tras la anastomosis. Evaluar siempre la perfusión del cabo proximal antes de confeccionar la anastomosis; considerar fluorescencia con indocianina (ICG) en casos dudosos.

blocks.title: Drenaje linfático y ganglios de resección mínima (≥12 ganglios)
blocks.content: El drenaje linfático del colon sigue el trayecto vascular en tres niveles: epicólico (pared colónica), paracólico (a lo largo de la arteria marginal), intermedio (sobre los pedículos principales) y apical (en el origen de la AMS o AMI). La escisión mesocólica completa (CME) con ligadura vascular central garantiza la resección en bloque de los ganglios del nivel intermedio y apical, que son los que con mayor frecuencia albergan metástasis en estadio III. El estándar NCCN/ESMO exige la identificación de ≥12 ganglios linfáticos en la pieza quirúrgica para una estadificación fiable; la cifra insuficiente obliga a considerar el estadio como pN indeterminado y puede llevar a subestadificación del 20–30% de los casos.

blocks.title: Identificación del nervio hipogástrico en cirugía rectal
blocks.content: Los nervios hipogástricos discurren sobre la fascia presacra en posición posterolateral al recto, visibles como dos cordones blanquecinos a 1–2 cm de la línea media. Se identifican mejor durante la disección posterior, inmediatamente después de la ligadura de la arteria rectal superior. Una disección demasiado lateral en este nivel — o la tracción excesiva sobre el recto — es la causa más frecuente de disfunción sexual y vesical postoperatoria en hombres jóvenes sometidos a TME. La visión directa y el uso de tracción controlada (no avulsión) son los principios protectores clave.

blocks.title: Diagnóstico y estadificación
blocks.content: El diagnóstico de cáncer colorrectal (CCR) en estadio III requiere un algoritmo de estadificación estandarizado que integra histología, imagen multimodal y biomarcadores. La colonoscopia completa con biopsia es el estudio inicial obligatorio: confirma la histología, localiza el tumor con precisión y descarta lesiones sincrónicas, las cuales ocurren en 3–5% de los casos. Una colonoscopia incompleta por obstrucción luminal debe ser completada postoperatoriamente, idealmente dentro de los 3–6 meses tras la resección. El antígeno carcinoembrionario (CEA) preoperatorio tiene valor pronóstico independiente y sirve como línea de base para la vigilancia oncológica; valores > 5 ng/mL se asocian con peor pronóstico incluso en tumores N+ resecables.

blocks.title: Imagen de estadificación: protocolo y selección de modalidad
blocks.content: La tomografía computarizada (TC) de tórax, abdomen y pelvis con contraste intravenoso es el pilar de la estadificación sistémica en CCR de colon. Identifica adenopatías regionales, enfermedad a distancia y compromiso de órganos adyacentes. Para el cáncer de recto, la resonancia magnética (RM) pélvica de alta resolución es el estudio de elección para la estadificación locorregional: define con precisión la distancia al margen circunferencial de resección (CRM), la invasión de la fascia mesorrectal, la extensión extramural venosa (EMVI) y el nivel de compromiso del esfínter. La tomografía por emisión de positrones (PET-TC) no está indicada de rutina en el estadio III operable, pero se reserva para casos con hallazgos indeterminados en TC, CEA elevado con imagen convencional negativa, o recurrencia sospechada en la vigilancia.

blocks.content: Error frecuente: Estadificar un cáncer de recto medio con TC pélvica sola. La TC tiene sensibilidad limitada para definir el CRM y la EMVI — dos variables que determinan si el paciente recibirá neoadyuvancia y si es candidato a cirugía de preservación de esfínter. Todo cáncer de recto clínicamente estadio II–III debe tener RM pélvica dedicada antes de cualquier decisión terapéutica.

blocks.content: Diferencia clave colon vs. recto en estadificación: En colon, el estadio se define por anatomía patológica (pTNM) sobre la pieza resecada. En recto, se trabaja con dos estadios distintos: el clínico pre-neoadyuvante (cTNM por RM) y el patológico post-neoadyuvante (ypTNM). La respuesta patológica completa (ypT0N0) tiene implicaciones pronósticas favorables y, en ciertos protocolos, habilita estrategias de 'watch and wait'. Documentar ambos estadios en el registro oncológico es obligatorio.

NCCN Guidelines Colon Cancer / Rectal Cancer (v.2024): La cosecha mínima de 12 ganglios linfáticos es estándar para una estadificación N adecuada. Un resultado pN0 con < 12 ganglios analizados debe registrarse como estadificación ganglionar insuficiente (pNx en la práctica). ESMO 2020 respalda RM pélvica como obligatoria en cáncer de recto antes de cualquier tratamiento, con reporte estructurado que incluya CRM, EMVI y nivel tumoral.

points: Colonoscopia completa + biopsia es el primer paso diagnóstico; el CEA preoperatorio tiene valor pronóstico y establece la línea de base para vigilancia.
TC de tórax/abdomen/pelvis es la estadificación sistémica estándar en colon; en recto, la RM pélvica de alta resolución es obligatoria para definir CRM, EMVI y planificación neoadyuvante.
El PET-TC no está indicado de rutina en estadio III operable — reservarlo para hallazgos indeterminados o sospecha de recurrencia.

El estadio III de colon se clasifica en subestadios IIIA–IIIC por combinaciones T1–T4b / N1–N2b (AJCC 8ª ed.); el subestadio determina la duración óptima de la quimioterapia adyuvante (3 vs. 6 meses, IDEA).
En recto: documentar siempre cTNM (pre-tratamiento por RM) y ypTNM (post-neoadyuvante en la pieza); ambos son clínicamente relevantes y pronósticos.
Una cosecha ganglionar < 12 nodos representa estadificación N inadecuada y puede llevar a subestadiaje — implicación directa en la decisión de adyuvancia.

blocks.title: Biomarcadores moleculares en cáncer colorrectal estadio III
blocks.content: El perfil molecular del tumor colorrectal en estadio III cumple una doble función: orientar las decisiones de tratamiento adyuvante y anticipar las opciones terapéuticas si la enfermedad progresa a estadio IV. El panel mínimo recomendado al diagnóstico incluye estado de reparación de errores de emparejamiento (MMR/MSI), mutaciones en RAS (KRAS/NRAS exones 2–4), mutación BRAF V600E y amplificación de HER2. La lateralidad tumoral — colon derecho versus izquierdo — añade un contexto pronóstico y predictivo que debe integrarse en la interpretación de estos marcadores. Omitir cualquiera de ellos en la pieza quirúrgica implica diferir decisiones que son tiempo-dependientes para el paciente.

blocks.title: RAS (KRAS/NRAS) y lateralidad tumoral
blocks.content: Las mutaciones en KRAS y NRAS (exones 2, 3 y 4) son el determinante negativo más relevante para el uso de anticuerpos anti-EGFR en enfermedad metastásica. En estadio III, estas mutaciones no modifican la indicación ni el esquema de quimioterapia adyuvante, pero su determinación en la pieza quirúrgica es obligatoria porque el ~30–50% de los estadios III eventualmente recaen y necesitarán una decisión terapéutica inmediata. La lateralidad añade una capa adicional: incluso en tumores RAS/RAF wild-type, los tumores del colon derecho presentan una respuesta inferior a los anti-EGFR en primera línea metastásica — el beneficio de cetuximab y panitumumab se concentra en tumores del lado izquierdo (colon descendente, sigma, recto). Esta interacción entre lateralidad y estado RAS debe comunicarse al paciente desde el estadio III como parte del pronóstico y la planificación de contingencias.

blocks.title: Error frecuente: no solicitar el panel molecular completo en la pieza quirúrgica
blocks.content: Un residente solicita solo MSI/MMR en la pieza de colectomía de un estadio III y difiere RAS, BRAF y HER2 'para cuando se necesiten'. Seis meses después, el paciente desarrolla metástasis hepáticas y la muestra original ya no está disponible en condiciones óptimas para retest. La biopsia de la metástasis es factible pero no siempre accesible. La determinación completa del panel molecular debe realizarse de forma sistemática e inmediata en la pieza quirúrgica de todo estadio III — no cuando el paciente progresa.

blocks.title: MSI-H / dMMR: determinación universal y síndrome de Lynch
blocks.content: La política de cribado universal de MMR — mediante inmunohistoquímica de las cuatro proteínas MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 y PMS2 en toda pieza de cáncer colorrectal — está respaldada por NCCN y ESMO como estándar de práctica, independientemente de la edad o el estadio. En estadio III, el 15–20% de los tumores son MSI-H/dMMR; la mayoría en el colon derecho. Ante la pérdida de MLH1, el siguiente paso crítico es determinar si se trata de un fenómeno esporádico (metilación del promotor de MLH1, asociado a BRAF V600E y perfil CIMP-alto) o una variante germinal (síndrome de Lynch). La coexistencia de MSI-H + BRAF V600E hace altamente improbable el síndrome de Lynch y debe desencadenar reflexivamente el análisis de metilación del promotor de MLH1, evitando derivaciones innecesarias a consejo genético germinal.

blocks.title: MSI-H + BRAF V600E: no es Lynch — actúa antes de derivar
blocks.content: Cuando un tumor MSI-H presenta simultáneamente mutación BRAF V600E, la probabilidad de síndrome de Lynch es <1–2%. El mecanismo es silenciamiento epigenético por metilación del promotor MLH1 (fenotipo CIMP-alto, esporádico). Solicitar el análisis de metilación de MLH1 antes de la derivación a genética evita una cadena de pruebas germinales innecesarias y reduce la ansiedad familiar. Esta distinción tiene implicaciones directas para el consejo familiar y el cribado de familiares de primer grado.

blocks.name: KEYNOTE-177
blocks.citation: André T, et al. Pembrolizumab in Microsatellite-Instability–High Advanced Colorectal Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:2207-2218.

blocks.intervention: Pembrolizumab vs quimioterapia estándar (FOLFOX4 o FOLFOX6 ± bevacizumab/cetuximab) en primera línea
blocks.result: Pembrolizumab mejoró significativamente la supervivencia libre de progresión frente a quimioterapia (PFS mediana 16,5 vs 8,2 meses; HR 0,60). Tasa de respuesta objetiva del 43,8% vs 33,1%.
blocks.practice_change: Pembrolizumab en monoterapia es el estándar de primera línea para CRC metastásico MSI-H/dMMR, consolidando MSI/MMR como biomarcador predictivo obligatorio en estadio IV — y justificando su determinación universal desde estadio III.

blocks.title: HER2 en estadio III: testar ahora, no cuando progrese
blocks.content: La amplificación de HER2 (~2–3% del CRC) es mutuamente excluyente con mutaciones en RAS y BRAF, y define una subpoblación que responde a tucatinib + trastuzumab (datos MOUNTAINEER) en enfermedad metastásica. En estadio III, no existe indicación adyuvante anti-HER2 actualmente. Sin embargo, la determinación debe realizarse en la pieza quirúrgica porque: (1) la biopsia de metástasis puede ser técnicamente difícil o mostrar heterogeneidad; (2) el resultado condiciona el algoritmo completo de líneas de tratamiento futuras. No esperes a que el paciente recaiga para solicitarla.

points: El panel molecular mínimo en estadio III incluye MMR/MSI, KRAS/NRAS (exones 2–4), BRAF V600E y HER2 — debe solicitarse en la pieza quirúrgica, no diferirse a la recaída.
MSI-H/dMMR en estadio III: fluoropirimidina en monoterapia está contraindicada como adyuvancia; FOLFOX/CAPOX sigue siendo el estándar.
MSI-H + BRAF V600E indica casi siempre CRC esporádico por metilación del promotor MLH1 — solicitar test de metilación antes de derivar a consejo genético germinal.
RAS/NRAS mutado excluye el uso de anti-EGFR en línea metastásica; incluso en RAS wild-type, el beneficio anti-EGFR se restringe a tumores del lado izquierdo.
KEYNOTE-177 estableció pembrolizumab como primera línea estándar en CRC metastásico MSI-H, justificando la determinación universal de MMR desde el diagnóstico quirúrgico.
HER2 amplificado (~2–3%) es accionable en estadio IV (MOUNTAINEER: tucatinib + trastuzumab); su determinación en estadio III es prospectiva y obligatoria para planificación oncológica.

sections.title: Tratamiento del cáncer de colon: cirugía y adyuvancia

blocks.title: Oncological Principles of Colectomy for Colon Cancer
blocks.content: Curative-intent surgery for colon cancer requires adherence to three non-negotiable oncological principles: complete mesocolic excision (CME), central vascular ligation (CVL), and harvest of ≥12 regional lymph nodes. CME—analogous to TME for rectal cancer—removes the intact mesocolon along embryological tissue planes, maximizing the lymphovascular envelope and reducing local recurrence. CVL at the vascular root ensures the highest nodal yield along the primary lymphatic drainage and achieves accurate pathological staging. An adequate lymph node harvest of ≥12 nodes is both a quality metric and a staging requirement: fewer than 12 nodes retrieved mandates explanation (prior chemotherapy, anatomical limitation, or poor surgical technique) and may lead to understaging, converting apparent Stage II disease to Stage III had additional nodes been examined. NCCN guidelines (v2024) identify <12 nodes as a high-risk feature in Stage II disease, with direct implications for adjuvant chemotherapy decision-making.

blocks.content: Laparoscopic colectomy is oncologically equivalent to open resection for colon cancer — but only when performed by a trained surgeon with adequate volume. The COST, COLOR, and CLASSIC trials established non-inferiority for colon primaries. The conversion rate in the CLASSIC rectal cohort (29%) and a higher positive circumferential resection margin rate should temper enthusiasm for laparoscopic rectal resection outside expert centers.

blocks.title: Adjuvant Chemotherapy: Stage II Risk Stratification and Stage III Standard
blocks.content: Adjuvant chemotherapy is the standard of care for all resected Stage III colon cancer. FOLFOX (oxaliplatin + fluorouracil/leucovorin) or CAPOX (capecitabine + oxaliplatin) are guideline-endorsed regimens with survival benefit established in multiple Phase III trials. For Stage II disease, adjuvant chemotherapy is NOT routinely recommended for low-risk patients, but is considered for high-risk Stage II features: T4 lesion, bowel obstruction or perforation at presentation, poorly differentiated histology (excluding MSI-H), perineural or lymphovascular invasion, <12 nodes examined, or positive/indeterminate margins. MSI-H status in Stage II disease specifically predicts lack of benefit from fluoropyrimidine monotherapy and is associated with favorable prognosis without chemotherapy — current NCCN/ESMO guidelines recommend against adjuvant 5-FU or capecitabine monotherapy in MSI-H Stage II tumors. When chemotherapy is offered in high-risk Stage II, the decision between FOLFOX and fluoropyrimidine monotherapy hinges on patient comorbidity, tolerance of oxaliplatin, and MSI status.

A resident orders adjuvant capecitabine monotherapy for a Stage II colon cancer patient with T3N0 disease and a single high-risk feature. The pathology returns MSI-H. This is a critical error: fluoropyrimidine monotherapy confers no benefit — and retrospective data suggest potential harm — in MSI-H tumors. If chemotherapy is indicated in MSI-H Stage II or Stage III disease, FOLFOX/CAPOX is the required backbone. Monotherapy with 5-FU or capecitabine alone is contraindicated in dMMR/MSI-H tumors.

points: CME with CVL and ≥12 lymph nodes harvested are the three non-negotiable oncological standards for curative colectomy; <12 nodes is both a staging failure and a high-risk feature triggering adjuvant chemotherapy consideration in Stage II disease.
Laparoscopic colectomy is oncologically equivalent to open resection for colon primaries (COST, COLOR, CLASSIC trials) and is the preferred approach at experienced centers.

All resected Stage III colon cancer patients should receive adjuvant FOLFOX or CAPOX; the IDEA collaboration established that 3 months of CAPOX is non-inferior to 6 months for low-risk Stage III (T1-3 N1), dramatically reducing peripheral neuropathy without compromising survival.
High-risk Stage III (T4 or N2) disease warrants 6 months of oxaliplatin-based therapy regardless of regimen choice.
MSI-H/dMMR tumors must NOT receive fluoropyrimidine monotherapy as adjuvant treatment in Stage II or Stage III disease — FOLFOX/CAPOX is the required standard when chemotherapy is indicated.

Prophylactic second-look surgery plus HIPEC is not standard of care for high-risk Stage III patients: PROPHYLOCHIP-PRODIGE 15 (Phase III, PMID 32717180) demonstrated no DFS benefit with this strategy.

sections.title: Tratamiento del cáncer de recto: estrategias neoadyuvantes

blocks.title: MRI-Based Risk Stratification: The Foundation of Rectal Cancer Treatment Planning
blocks.content: Modern rectal cancer management begins with high-resolution pelvic MRI to define the relationship of the tumor to the mesorectal fascia (MRF), extramural vascular invasion (EMVI), and nodal status. This imaging-based risk stratification — not clinical T/N stage alone — determines whether neoadjuvant therapy is indicated and what intensity is appropriate. The key categories are: low-risk (MRF-negative, no EMVI, cT1-3a N0), intermediate-risk (MRF-threatened but not involved, or cT3b-c N1-2 without worrisome features), and high/very-high-risk (MRF-involved, T4b, lateral nodal disease, or EMVI-positive). Patients with low-risk disease by MRI criteria may proceed directly to surgery without neoadjuvant therapy, a principle now firmly embedded in ESMO and NCCN guidelines.

blocks.title: Total Neoadjuvant Therapy: Rationale and Sequencing
blocks.content: Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) consolidates all systemic chemotherapy into the preoperative window, addressing both local disease (via radiosensitization) and occult micrometastatic disease earlier in the treatment course. Two sequencing strategies exist: induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy (induction TNT, as in PRODIGE 23), and short-course radiotherapy followed by consolidation chemotherapy before surgery (consolidation TNT, as in RAPIDO). Both approaches improve pathologic complete response (pCR) rates compared to conventional long-course CRT alone, but their impact on distant metastasis-free survival and overall survival differs in nuance. Importantly, TNT does not appear to compromise surgical outcomes or R0 resection rates when appropriately applied to high-risk disease.

blocks.name: RAPIDO
blocks.citation: Bahadoer RR et al. Lancet Oncol. 2021;22(1):29-42.
blocks.population: Locally advanced rectal cancer with high-risk MRI features (mrT4a/b, mrEMVI+, mrN2, threatened MRF, or lateral node+)
blocks.intervention: Short-course RT (5×5 Gy) → consolidation CAPOX or FOLFOX (18 weeks) → TME vs. long-course CRT (50.4 Gy + capecitabine) → optional adjuvant chemotherapy → TME
blocks.result: 3-year disease-related treatment failure: 23.7% (TNT arm) vs. 30.4% (standard arm); pCR rate 28.4% vs. 14.3%
blocks.practice_change: TNT with short-course RT + consolidation chemotherapy became the preferred strategy for high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer, displacing standard long-course CRT as the benchmark.

blocks.name: PRODIGE 23
blocks.citation: Conroy T et al. Lancet Oncol. 2021;22(5):702-715.
blocks.population: Locally advanced rectal cancer (cT3-4 M0), fit for oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy
blocks.intervention: Induction mFOLFIRINOX (6 cycles) → long-course CRT → TME → adjuvant FOLFOX vs. long-course CRT alone → TME → adjuvant FOLFOX
blocks.result: 3-year disease-free survival: 75.7% (TNT arm) vs. 68.5% (standard arm); pCR rate 27.5% vs. 11.7%
blocks.practice_change: Induction FOLFIRINOX before chemoradiotherapy improved DFS and pCR rates in locally advanced rectal cancer, establishing induction TNT as a viable alternative sequencing strategy to consolidation TNT.

blocks.name: PROSPECT
blocks.citation: Schrag D et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(4):322-334.
blocks.population: Low-risk locally advanced rectal cancer: cT2N1, cT3N0, or cT3N1 with MRF-negative tumors amenable to sphincter-preserving resection
blocks.intervention: Neoadjuvant FOLFOX (6 cycles) with selective CRT only if <20% tumor regression → TME → adjuvant FOLFOX vs. standard long-course CRT → TME → adjuvant FOLFOX
blocks.result: 5-year DFS: 80.8% (FOLFOX arm) vs. 78.6% (CRT arm); local recurrence rates were non-inferior; RT omitted in 89% of the FOLFOX arm
blocks.practice_change: Selective omission of radiotherapy using FOLFOX-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy is non-inferior to standard CRT in carefully selected low-risk rectal cancer, sparing the majority of eligible patients from pelvic RT toxicity.

blocks.scenario: A 48-year-old woman presents with a cT3N1 mid-rectal adenocarcinoma. Pelvic MRI shows the tumor 2 mm from the MRF (threatened), no EMVI, and two perirectal nodes measuring 8 mm with irregular borders. She has no peritoneal disease on staging CT. Her performance status is excellent and she is motivated to avoid a permanent colostomy.
blocks.discussion: This patient falls in the intermediate-to-high-risk category by MRI criteria (threatened MRF, N1 disease). She is a candidate for TNT rather than CRT alone, given the MRF threat and N1 status. Either RAPIDO-style (short-course RT → consolidation FOLFOX/CAPOX) or PRODIGE 23-style (induction FOLFIRINOX → CRT) is appropriate. A critical secondary goal in this patient is achieving sufficient downstaging to permit sphincter-preserving surgery — making pCR assessment and possible watch-and-wait strategy (OPRA criteria) a relevant shared decision-making discussion at baseline.

blocks.title: Watch & Wait After cCR: The OPRA Framework
blocks.content: The OPRA trial (Garcia-Aguilar et al., J Clin Oncol 2022) demonstrated that among patients achieving a clinical complete response (cCR) after TNT, approximately 40% can avoid surgery with a watch-and-wait strategy, with 3-year organ preservation rates of 58% (consolidation TNT) vs. 43% (induction TNT). Organ preservation should only be offered through a structured surveillance protocol: digital rectal exam + endoscopy every 3 months for 2 years. Critically, ~25% of patients who initially achieve cCR will develop local regrowth, and >90% of regrowths are still salvageable with surgery — making rigorous surveillance non-negotiable, not optional.

blocks.title: Do Not Apply TNT Protocols to Low-Risk Rectal Cancer
blocks.content: A resident orders neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX + CRT for a cT3N0 upper rectal tumor with a clear MRF on MRI. This overtreats the patient: upper rectal low-risk tumors may not require any neoadjuvant therapy, and intermediate/low-risk tumors with clear MRF may be candidates for PROSPECT-style selective RT omission. TNT carries cumulative toxicity — specifically grade 3+ peripheral neuropathy and hematologic toxicity — that is only justified when the risk-benefit ratio favors aggressive downstaging. Always reassess the MRI risk tier before selecting a neoadjuvant regimen.

points: MRI-based risk stratification (MRF status, EMVI, T/N category) is the essential first step; clinical T/N stage alone is insufficient to guide neoadjuvant therapy selection in rectal cancer.

TNT (total neoadjuvant therapy) improves pCR rates and disease-related treatment failure compared to standard CRT in high-risk disease — RAPIDO (consolidation) and PRODIGE 23 (induction) are the two landmark protocols.

PROSPECT established that selective RT omission using neoadjuvant FOLFOX is non-inferior to CRT in low-risk rectal cancer (clear MRF, cT2-3N0-1), sparing RT toxicity in the majority of eligible patients.

Watch-and-wait after clinical complete response (cCR) is a valid organ-preservation strategy per OPRA criteria, but requires structured, protocol-driven surveillance every 3 months — regrowth occurs in ~25% and demands prompt surgical salvage.

MSI-H/dMMR status is particularly relevant in rectal cancer being considered for immunotherapy-based neoadjuvant approaches (investigational), and should be assessed at diagnosis alongside RAS/BRAF profiling.

Short-course RT (5×5 Gy) followed by consolidation chemotherapy (RAPIDO) and long-course CRT preceded by induction FOLFIRINOX (PRODIGE 23) are both acceptable TNT strategies for high/very-high-risk disease — choice should be individualized by multidisciplinary team discussion.

blocks.title: Tratamiento de la Enfermedad Metastásica (mCRC): Principios Generales
blocks.content: El manejo del cáncer colorrectal metastásico (mCRC) requiere una estrategia secuencial y personalizada basada en el perfil molecular del tumor, la carga y distribución de la enfermedad, y el estado funcional del paciente. La selección del esquema de primera línea debe integrar el estado de RAS/BRAF, MSI/MMR, HER2, y la lateralidad tumoral antes de iniciar cualquier tratamiento sistémico. La distinción entre enfermedad potencialmente resecable y no resecable en el momento del diagnóstico determina si el objetivo del tratamiento es conversión a resecabilidad (con intención curativa) o control paliativo de la enfermedad. El tumor board multidisciplinar con cirujano hepatobiliar, oncólogo médico, y radiólogo intervencionista es esencial desde la primera visita.

blocks.title: Pembrolizumab vs. Quimioterapia en Primera Línea MSI-H/dMMR mCRC
blocks.population: Pacientes con mCRC MSI-H/dMMR no tratados previamente
blocks.intervention: Pembrolizumab 200 mg cada 3 semanas vs. elección del investigador (FOLFOX o FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab o cetuximab)
blocks.result: Mediana de PFS: 16,5 meses con pembrolizumab vs. 8,2 meses con quimioterapia (HR 0,60; p=0,0002). Tasa de respuesta objetiva: 43,8% vs. 33,1%. Beneficio en OS confirmado en actualización.
blocks.practice_change: Pembrolizumab en monoterapia reemplaza la quimioterapia estándar como tratamiento de primera línea en todos los pacientes con mCRC MSI-H/dMMR.

La quimioterapia no es el estándar de primera línea en este subgrupo — la ventana terapéutica de máximo beneficio inmunológico se pierde si se expone primero a quimioterapia. Solicitar siempre el estado MMR/MSI antes del inicio de cualquier línea sistémica.

blocks.title: Enfermedad Hepática Resecable: Estrategia Quirúrgica
blocks.content: Las metástasis hepáticas aisladas o predominantes ocurren en aproximadamente el 15–25% de los pacientes con mCRC y representan el único escenario con potencial curativo en enfermedad metastásica. La resección R0 con margen negativo es el objetivo; márgenes de 1 mm son aceptables si se preserve función hepática adecuada. La elección entre resección simultánea (colorrectal + hepática en mismo acto) vs. estadificada depende de la carga hepática, el estado del paciente y la complejidad técnica: resecciones hepáticas mayores (≥3 segmentos) se estadifican habitualmente. En enfermedad hepática contralateral que compromete el volumen hepático futuro remanente (FLR <25–30% en hígado sano, <40% tras quimioterapia), la embolización de la vena porta (PVE) o el ALPPS (Associating Liver Partition and Portal Vein Ligation for Staged Hepatectomy) permite hipertrofia del lóbulo contralateral, aunque ALPPS conlleva mayor morbimortalidad perioperatoria que la PVE convencional y debe reservarse para centros de alto volumen.

ALPPS genera hipertrofia hepática más rápida que la PVE (2–3 semanas vs. 4–8 semanas), pero la morbilidad mayor (Clavien-Dindo ≥III) es significativamente superior. La indicación óptima de ALPPS es el paciente con FLR insuficiente para PVE convencional, tumor bilobular sin respuesta a quimioterapia, y ventana de resecabilidad corta. Nunca debe ofrecerse como primera opción técnica.

blocks.name: PROPHYLOCHIP-PRODIGE 15
blocks.title: Cirugía de Second-Look + HIPEC vs. Vigilancia en Pacientes de Alto Riesgo de Metástasis Peritoneales
blocks.population: Pacientes con cáncer colorrectal de alto riesgo de desarrollar metástasis peritoneales (ovario resecado, perforación tumoral, metástasis peritoneales mínimas resecadas en la cirugía índice)
blocks.intervention: Cirugía de second-look + HIPEC (oxaliplatino) a los 6 meses de la cirugía índice vs. vigilancia estándar con imagen
blocks.result: No se demostró beneficio estadísticamente significativo en supervivencia libre de enfermedad (DFS) con la estrategia intervencionista frente a vigilancia. La cirugía profiláctica añadió morbilidad sin mejorar el pronóstico oncológico.
blocks.practice_change: La cirugía de second-look profiláctica más HIPEC NO debe ofrecerse de forma estándar a pacientes de alto riesgo de Stage III/mCRC fuera de ensayo clínico.
blocks.citation: PROPHYLOCHIP-PRODIGE 15 — Arjona-Sánchez A et al., Lancet Oncol 2020. PMID 32717180

blocks.content: PRECAUCIÓN EN EXTRAPOLACIÓN: La revisión JAMA Oncology 2021 (PMID 33956063) analiza HIPEC conjuntamente en cáncer de ovario y colorrectal peritoneal. Los datos favorables de HIPEC en cáncer de ovario (OVHIPEC-1) NO son transferibles al CRC peritoneal — son enfermedades biológicamente distintas con quimiosensibilidades diferentes. En mCRC con carcinomatosis peritoneal, la evidencia de HIPEC se basa en el ensayo PRODIGE 7, que no demostró beneficio añadido de HIPEC sobre citorreducción completa sola.

blocks.title: Puntos Clave: Tratamiento del mCRC
points: El perfil molecular completo (RAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR, HER2) y la lateralidad tumoral deben conocerse ANTES de iniciar cualquier línea sistémica — determinan el régimen óptimo de primera línea.
MSI-H/dMMR mCRC: pembrolizumab en monoterapia es el estándar de primera línea (KEYNOTE-177; PFS 16,5 vs. 8,2 meses), superando a la quimioterapia convencional.
BRAF V600E en mCRC confiere pronóstico adverso; FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab en primera línea seguido de triplete BEACON (encorafenib + binimetinib + cetuximab) en progresión es la secuencia estándar.

Las metástasis hepáticas resecables deben evaluarse en tumor board con cirujano hepatobiliar; la resección R0 es el único escenario curativo en mCRC. ALPPS y PVE son herramientas de conversión de FLR insuficiente, no de primera elección.
PROPHYLOCHIP-PRODIGE 15 (PMID 32717180): la cirugía de second-look profiláctica + HIPEC no mejora la DFS en pacientes de alto riesgo y NO es estándar fuera de ensayo clínico.

Los datos de HIPEC en cáncer de ovario (PMID 33956063) no son extrapolables a CRC peritoneal — evitar razonar por analogía entre estas dos entidades al asesorar a pacientes con carcinomatosis colorrectal.

blocks.title: Oncologic Principles of Colorectal Resection
blocks.content: The oncologic goals of colorectal resection are threefold: complete removal of the primary tumor with clear radial and longitudinal margins (R0), resection of the regional lymphatic basin to its vascular origin, and preservation of the autonomic nervous system to maintain urinary and sexual function. Achieving R0 status is the single strongest surgeon-modifiable determinant of locoregional recurrence. In Stage III disease, where nodal positivity is already established, the adequacy of lymphadenectomy — defined by ≥12 lymph nodes harvested — directly impacts staging accuracy, guides adjuvant chemotherapy decisions, and may confer independent survival benefit through removal of occult nodal disease. Failure to meet this threshold should prompt pathologic re-examination before concluding nodal assessment is complete.

blocks.title: Right Hemicolectomy: Vascular Anatomy and D3 Lymphadenectomy
blocks.content: The ileocolic artery is the primary vascular pedicle for right hemicolectomy and must be ligated at its origin from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) to achieve a D3 (complete mesocolic excision, CME) dissection. Early identification of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) provides the medial-to-lateral dissection plane; the embryologic fusion plane between the mesocolon and the retroperitoneum (Toldt's fascia) is avascular and should be developed bluntly. High ligation of the right colic artery (when present) and the right branch of the middle colic artery extends the lymphadenectomy to the central nodes. CME with central vascular ligation has been associated with higher nodal yield and lower locoregional recurrence rates compared to conventional right hemicolectomy in observational data, though randomized Level I evidence remains limited. Medial-to-lateral dissection reduces the risk of inadvertent duodenal and retroperitoneal injury compared to lateral-to-medial approaches.

A resident ligates what appears to be the ileocolic artery early in the dissection without first identifying the SMV. If the SMV has not been positively confirmed, the structure being ligated may be the SMV itself or a jejunal branch — catastrophic venous infarction can result. Always identify and trace the SMV before any pedicle ligation during right hemicolectomy.

blocks.title: Left Hemicolectomy and Sigmoid Resection: IMA Ligation and Ureter Identification
blocks.content: The central controversy in left-sided colonic resection is the level of inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) ligation: high tie (flush at the aorta, distal to the left colic artery origin) versus low tie (preservation of the left colic artery, ligation distal to it). High ligation maximizes nodal harvest along the IMA trunk — the D3 territory — and provides greater colonic mobilization for a tension-free anastomosis. Low ligation theoretically preserves perfusion to the anastomosis via the left colic artery, but current evidence does not consistently demonstrate a reduction in anastomotic leak rates that would justify compromising nodal clearance in Stage III disease. The left ureter and gonadal vessels are at greatest risk during IMA ligation and must be positively identified before any ligation is performed; they lie in the retroperitoneum just lateral to the IMA origin. Failure to identify the ureter before dividing pedicles accounts for a significant proportion of iatrogenic ureteral injuries in colorectal surgery.

For left hemicolectomy, enter the avascular retroperitoneal plane medially at the IMA origin before mobilizing the splenic flexure. Identifying the left ureter from a medial approach — while it is still attached to the retroperitoneum and Gerota's fascia — is far safer than searching for it after lateral mobilization has disrupted the tissue planes.

blocks.title: Total Mesorectal Excision: Sharp Dissection and Nerve Preservation
blocks.content: Total mesorectal excision (TME) is the anatomic standard for rectal cancer resection and requires sharp dissection in the holy plane — the areolar tissue between the visceral (mesorectal) fascia and the parietal (presacral) fascia — under direct vision throughout. Blunt or finger dissection tears the mesorectal envelope, creates positive circumferential resection margins (CRM), and seeds the surgical field with tumor deposits. The mesorectal fascia must remain intact on the specimen; a defect or incomplete dissection mandates intraoperative reassessment. Autonomic nerve preservation requires identification and protection of the superior hypogastric plexus at the IMA origin, the hypogastric nerves at the sacral promontory, and the pelvic nerve plexus (S2–S4) lateral to the rectum at the level of the seminal vesicles or vagina. Lateral dissection is the most common site of pelvic nerve injury and should always be performed under direct vision, staying medial to the neurovascular bundles.

blocks.scenario: A 54-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic low anterior resection with TME for a T3N1 rectal cancer at 8 cm from the anal verge. The pathology report returns noting 'incomplete mesorectal excision' with a defect in the mesorectal fascia and a CRM of 0.8 mm. The patient has not received neoadjuvant therapy.
blocks.discussion: This is a positive or near-positive CRM (<1 mm) resulting from incomplete TME — a direct technical failure. In the absence of neoadjuvant radiotherapy, this patient is at high risk for locoregional recurrence and should be referred urgently to a multidisciplinary team for discussion of adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy and systemic chemotherapy. The operative report should be reviewed for the anatomic level at which the plane was lost; lateral dissection and the anterior peritoneal reflection are the most common sites of mesorectal envelope violation. This case illustrates why TME quality — judged by the pathologist on fresh specimen — is a measurable surgical quality indicator.

blocks.content: After firing a circular stapler for a low colorectal anastomosis, always perform intraoperative air-leak testing (transanal insufflation with the pelvis filled with saline) before closing. A visible air leak mandates intraoperative repair or conversion to a Hartmann's procedure — do not rely on a defunctioning stoma alone to manage a technically failed anastomosis.

points: R0 resection with ≥12 lymph nodes harvested is the surgical floor for Stage III CRC — nodal count below this threshold mandates pathologic re-examination before staging is finalized.
During right hemicolectomy, identify the SMV before ligating any pedicle; medial-to-lateral dissection in Toldt's plane minimizes retroperitoneal injury.
High IMA ligation (D3) is preferred in left-sided resection for Stage III disease to maximize nodal clearance; the left ureter must be positively identified before any ligation.

TME requires sharp dissection in the holy plane with an intact mesorectal envelope — incomplete excision with a positive or near-positive CRM (<1 mm) is a surgically preventable cause of locoregional recurrence.

Defunctioning loop ileostomy is mandatory for anastomoses ≤6 cm from the anal verge and for all anastomoses following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy; it reduces the clinical consequence of leak but does not replace technical anastomotic quality.
Intraoperative air-leak testing after stapled colorectal anastomosis is a non-negotiable quality step — a positive leak requires immediate intraoperative management, not expectant observation.

blocks.title: Anastomotic Leak: Incidence, Diagnosis, and Classification
blocks.content: Anastomotic leak (AL) remains the most feared postoperative complication following colorectal resection, with incidence directly correlated to anastomotic level. Ileocolic and right colonic anastomoses carry a leak rate of 1–3%, while left colonic anastomoses approach 3–6% and low rectal anastomoses (within 5–7 cm of the anal verge) range from 10–20% even with defunctioning stoma. CT scan with rectal contrast or water-soluble enema is the diagnostic modality of choice when clinical suspicion arises — fever, leukocytosis, and tachycardia on postoperative days 3–7 should prompt immediate imaging rather than watchful waiting. The Hinchey classification, originally developed for diverticular perforation, is routinely adapted for post-anastomotic contamination: Grade I (pericolic/mesorectal abscess), Grade II (pelvic abscess), Grade III (purulent peritonitis), Grade IV (fecal peritonitis). This grading directly guides the choice between percutaneous drainage, endoluminal vacuum therapy, or return to the operating room.

blocks.content: A resident reassures the team that a low-grade fever on POD 4 after a low anterior resection 'is expected after pelvic dissection' and defers imaging. This is a dangerous pattern — AL after LAR peaks on POD 3–7 and subtle signs (persistent tachycardia >90, CRP >150 mg/L on POD 3–5, failure to tolerate diet) mandate CT with rectal contrast before clinical deterioration into Hinchey III/IV. Early diagnosis preserves the anastomosis; delayed diagnosis forces a Hartmann.

blocks.title: Postoperative Ileus vs. Mechanical Small Bowel Obstruction
blocks.content: Distinguishing postoperative ileus (POI) from early mechanical small bowel obstruction (SBO) is a high-stakes clinical decision in the first 3–5 postoperative days. POI is universal following abdominal surgery, driven by surgical handling, opioid use, and neurogenic inhibition; it typically resolves within 3–5 days with return of flatus and bowel sounds. Early SBO — caused by adhesions, internal herniation through mesenteric defects, or port-site hernias — presents with colicky pain, dilated loops on CT with a transition point, and absent or high-pitched bowel sounds. CT with oral and IV contrast is the definitive diagnostic tool and should not be delayed if obstruction is suspected beyond POD 5. A mesenteric defect herniation (particularly after laparoscopic resection where the mesenteric window was not closed) can progress rapidly to strangulation — a closed-loop obstruction on CT mandates urgent operative intervention regardless of symptom duration.

After laparoscopic right hemicolectomy, always close the mesenteric defect to prevent internal herniation — a technically minor step that prevents a potentially catastrophic closed-loop obstruction. If a patient presents with postoperative SBO and CT shows a 'swirl sign' or mesenteric torsion, do not attempt prolonged conservative management. Time to OR is the determinant of bowel viability.
